design_detail: Narrative review (Frontiers in Genetics, 12 November 2012, volume 3, article number 235, as printed in the citation line on the PMC page) by four authors from one research group, using MDMA and methamphetamine as two examples of how CYP2D6 genetics might matter for amphetamine-type drugs. About 3,300 words of main text in ten headed sections (editors' count), one table of 21 compounds with in vitro enzyme constants (Table 1, read as text), two metabolic schemes (Figures 1 and 2, images not viewed) and 56 references. No methods section: no databases, search dates, terms or selection rules; no pooled estimate. The four sections on MDMA alone hold about 1,300 words and the three on methamphetamine alone about 700; the rest is shared (introduction, background, conclusions). The methamphetamine sections were read and are summarized only briefly, because the library claims built from this card concern MDMA.
can_establish: What one research group concluded about how MDMA interacts with CYP2D6 (as substrate and as an enzyme-inactivating inhibitor), which primary studies it points to for genotype comparisons, for the effect of CYP2D6-blocking antidepressants on MDMA levels and for severe reactions with ritonavir, and how it reads that evidence as a whole.
cannot_establish: The size of any effect of CYP2D6 genotype or of CYP2D6-blocking medicines on MDMA exposure or on harm (almost no numbers are given for the genotype comparisons); how many people have their enzyme blocked by one dose (the two fractions given are 67% of men and 100% of women, from two studies not read here); whether MAOIs cause life-threatening reactions with MDMA (no MAOI source can be told from the citations); or whether CYP2D6 genotype changes the risk of death.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). No databases, search dates, terms or inclusion criteria are reported. The Introduction says the review will look at available clinical data against three postulates and chooses MDMA and methamphetamine as two archetypes (Introduction, 4th paragraph).
sample.demographics: Not applicable. Sample sizes of cited studies, where the text gives them: nine extensive metabolizers (six *1/*1, three *1/*4) compared with poor metabolizers (*4/*4) after two consecutive doses (MDMA and CYP2D6 pharmacogenetics, 1st paragraph; the reference-list title of one source says one poor metabolizer and nine extensive metabolizers); for methamphetamine, 8 extensive and 3 poor metabolizers given 10 mg by mouth, 202 patients and 337 controls in a Japanese genotype study, 18 autopsies and 52 people who use methamphetamine.
sample.selection_effects: No stated search, so completeness cannot be judged. At least 15 of 56 references are by the authors' group, including the studies behind the figures for enzyme inactivation, the paroxetine probe study and the ritonavir case. The authors state their belief (no data) that poor metabolizers are under-represented among people who use MDMA because of the strong effects they feel (section 'CYP2D6, MDMA, and methamphetamine: background considerations', 4th paragraph); if true, genotype comparisons in such groups are biased.

exposure.measurement: Not applicable. Cited studies describe CYP2D6 status by genotype (alleles such as *4/*4, *1/*4, *1/*10) or by activity group (poor, intermediate, extensive, ultrarapid); genotyping and phenotyping methods are not given.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: a single dose and two consecutive doses of MDMA, 10 mg of methamphetamine by mouth, and antidepressants given before MDMA. No milligram doses are given for the MDMA studies.
exposure.polysubstance: Not discussed for the intoxication series and the ritonavir and MAOI reports.

comparison.controls: Not applicable. Comparisons described are between genotype groups (poor against extensive metabolizers after two doses; reduced-activity genotypes against others for sodium and cortisol) and, for methamphetamine, patients against controls.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: The authors suggest that people with strong effects (poor metabolizers) stop or limit use, so genotype frequencies among people who use MDMA may differ from the general population (their belief, not tested).

outcomes.instruments: Not applicable (cited studies). Quantities mentioned: plasma MDMA and its metabolite HMMA; recovery of urinary thioether adducts; plasma osmolality, sodium and vasopressin; plasma cortisol; CYP2D6 activity after a dose (the basis of the 'phenocopying' figures); neuropsychological performance after methamphetamine.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Phenocopying' is used for the measured activity of CYP2D6 falling, after a dose of MDMA, to the level typical of poor metabolizers whatever the genotype (section 'MDMA CYP2D6 mechanism-based inhibition and the phenocopying phenomenon', one paragraph).

analysis.effect_sizes: No pooled estimates. Figures quoted from other work: enzyme inactivation within about 2 hours and recovery to the starting level after at least 10 days; phenocopying in 67% of men and 100% of women; metabolic clearance about 75% of plasma clearance, of which about 30% regulated by CYP2D6 (also written 'less than 30%', and 'lower than 50%' of metabolic clearance); MDMA concentrations changed by 15 to 30% (the sentence lacks a verb) and the metabolite HMMA 40 to 50% lower with paroxetine, reboxetine or duloxetine; in vitro intrinsic clearance of the *1 enzyme variant 123 times that of *10 for MDMA O-demethylenation (67 and 157 times for two methamphetamine reactions); Km 2.2 against 39.6 micromol/L for MDMA and methamphetamine (Table 1).
analysis.selective_reporting: Not assessable: no search or selection method. The Introduction promises to see how far three postulates were confirmed; the Concluding remarks do not go through them one by one.

interpretation_gap.results_show: As described by the review, two laboratory studies (one in men, one in women) found CYP2D6 activity reduced to a poor-metabolizer level after one dose of MDMA in 67% of the men and in all of the women. A few small studies compared genotype groups for blood levels, temperature, sodium and cortisol; in a series of poisonings the authors say poor-metabolizer genotypes were not over-represented. Antidepressants that block CYP2D6 raised MDMA levels by a fraction of the order of 15 to 30% and lowered HMMA, and severe or fatal reactions with ritonavir are cited to case reports. No numbers are given for the genotype comparisons.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says that everyone, whatever the genotype, is turned into a poor metabolizer by MDMA, that the CYP2D6 share of clearance is substantially lower than in vitro work predicts, and that the clinical relevance of CYP2D6 genetics is lower than predicted. The Concluding remarks add that carriers of reduced-function alleles are at higher risk of heightened effects and acute toxicity, including death, and that MAOIs and ritonavir are the main cause of life-threatening interactions with MDMA. 'Everyone' is stronger than the 67% found in men; the in vitro expectation is never stated, so 'lower than predicted' cannot be checked; and no data on toxicity or deaths by genotype, or on MAOIs, accompany the last statements.

timeline.event: De la Torre et al.: MDMA exposure rises more than in proportion to dose; the review takes from it and from a 2005 paroxetine study the figures of about 75% metabolic clearance and 30% CYP2D6 share
Segura et al. gave paroxetine as a CYP2D6 probe, and de la Torre et al. compared one CYP2D6 poor metabolizer with nine extensive metabolizers (both as cited in this review; neither read)

O'Mathuna et al. gave dextromethorphan as a CYP2D6 probe to 15 healthy men before and after MDMA: the urinary ratio rose above the poor-metabolizer cut-off in 10 of 15 men (the review's 67%), the first probe dose was given 4 hours after MDMA, and the ratio had not fully recovered at 10 days (read in full for this library, see its own card)
Yubero-Lahoz et al. in women (phenocopying in all, as described in this review; not read)
Schmid et al., pooled analysis of 139 healthy people: peak MDMA 15% higher in seven poor metabolizers, in the first three hours only
Sarparast et al. systematic review of medicine interactions with MDMA, which repeats the self-inhibition account second-hand

replication.where_it_stands: The main message (a small effect of CYP2D6 genotype on MDMA exposure, because MDMA blocks the enzyme itself) agrees with the 2016 pooled analysis, which was read in full for this library, and the enzyme-blocking finding agrees in direction with the 2008 probe-drug study in 15 men, also read in full. The 67% figure is 10 of 15 men; the 100% for women and the 2011 study were not read. The review's 'within 2 hours' timing is not what the 2008 study measured (first probe dose at 4 hours). The review's figures for antidepressants rest on four primary studies, of which only the 2007 paroxetine trial was read for this library (it gives a 16% rise in peak MDMA and 38 to 49% lower HMMA); the fractions of people whose enzyme is blocked and the reports of severe reactions rest on this narrative review and on case reports and studies not read here.

funding.funder: No funding statement appears in the page text read.
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare no commercial or financial relationships that could be construed as a conflict of interest.
funding.affiliations_note: Affiliation numbers 1 to 3 are printed beside the authors' names; the affiliation text was in a collapsed panel and was not read. The authors are members of the group that ran several of the clinical studies reviewed (at least 15 of 56 references). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the review.

what_would_settle_it: A genotyped, blinded crossover in which women and men with no, reduced and normal CYP2D6 function take the same MDMA dose once and, in another arm, twice in a session, with CYP2D6 probe activity measured before, at 2 hours, at 1 day and at 10 days; temperature, sodium and vasopressin recorded; and a registry of emergency presentations with genotype and co-taken medicines.

domains.note: No databases, search dates, terms or inclusion rules; the review does not say how its 56 references were chosen.

None. Small or single-person studies are written in the plural (poor-metabolizer 'subjects'), results are given without numbers, and an in vitro paper is cited for an observation in people (Kreth et al., 2000, by its reference-list title).

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: At least 15 of 56 references are by the authors' group, including the sources of the phenocopying fractions, the paroxetine probe study and the ritonavir case.

Several statements are marked as belief or 'probably' (poor metabolizers under-represented; effects lowered by transporter competition), but the Concluding remarks state higher risk of toxicity, including death, in reduced-function carriers without any data, and the abstract states that everyone is phenocopied against the text's own 67% in men.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for and against a clinical role of CYP2D6 genetics
domains.note: Findings pointing both ways are named (sodium and cortisol differences by genotype; no excess of poor-metabolizer genotypes in poisonings), but none is weighed with numbers, and the conclusion leans to the small-effect reading.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS 5.3); the editors' narrative-review checklist is used. The review can be cited for the authors' account of MDMA as an enzyme-inactivating inhibitor of CYP2D6 and for pointers to primary studies; every number in it is second-hand and unchecked, so a claim that rests on it alone stays at draft.

key_findings.finding: CYP2D6 is a small part of liver enzyme content (1 to 2% of total cytochrome P450) but handles an estimated 20 to 30% of marketed medicines, which the review lists as tricyclic and SSRI antidepressants, opioids, antipsychotics, antiemetics, antiarrhythmics and amphetamine-like drugs. About 5 to 10% of white people are poor metabolizers (lack two functional alleles); the four activity groups are poor, intermediate, extensive and ultrarapid metabolizers.
key_findings.locator: CYP2D6, MDMA, and methamphetamine: background considerations, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: MDMA is both a substrate of CYP2D6 (O-demethylenation to HHMA, then methylation to HMMA) and a potent mechanism-based inhibitor: the review gives metabolic clearance as about 75% of MDMA plasma clearance, with about 30% of its metabolism regulated by CYP2D6 (citing the 2000 non-linear pharmacokinetics paper and a 2005 paroxetine-probe study). Elsewhere the share is written as less than 30% (Drug-drug interactions, 1st paragraph) and, for metabolic clearance of both drugs, lower than 50% (Concluding remarks, 5th paragraph).
key_findings.locator: MDMA pharmacology and metabolic disposition, 4th paragraph; Drug-drug interactions, 1st paragraph; Concluding remarks, 5th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Mechanism-based inhibition happens shortly after a single dose, inactivating most liver CYP2D6 within about 2 hours with activity back to its starting level only after at least 10 days (citing studies from 2008, read separately for this library, and 2011, not read). The review says phenocopying (the enzyme behaving as in a poor metabolizer whatever the genotype) was seen in 67% of male subjects in one study and 100% of females in another, and infers that people who take repeated doses in a session face a higher chance of relative overdose and of adverse effects from other CYP2D6 substrates (citing a 2004 repeated-dose study). No clinical outcome of that inference is shown.
key_findings.locator: MDMA CYP2D6 mechanism-based inhibition and the phenocopying phenomenon, paragraph 1

key_findings.finding: Genotype comparisons are described without numbers: poor metabolizers (*4/*4) are said to show higher MDMA levels and more hyperthermia after a single dose (no citation on that sentence), extensive metabolizers (six *1/*1, three *1/*4) after two consecutive doses are said to resemble poor metabolizers, reduced-activity genotypes are linked to larger falls in plasma sodium and rises in vasopressin (a 2012 study) and some poor/intermediate genotypes to larger rises in cortisol (a 2012 study), and in a series of poisonings an excess of poor-metabolizer genotypes was not found.

Other enzymes contribute: CYP1A2 and, less, CYP2B6 and CYP3A4 can oxidize MDMA and MDA; CYP1A2 activity rose after MDMA in a 2012 study while CYP2D6 fell; in a paroxetine trial MDMA was still converted to HHMA, suggesting alternative pathways.

Antidepressants that block CYP2D6 (paroxetine, reboxetine, duloxetine) are said to change MDMA concentrations by 15 to 30% (the sentence has no verb; the direction is read as an increase from the next sentence and from the cited trials) and to lower the metabolite HMMA by 40 to 50%, while the effects of MDMA are lower, 'probably' because of competition for the uptake transporter (four citations: 2005, 2007, 2011, 2012).

The review states that ritonavir (an antiretroviral and CYP2D6 inhibitor) and MAO inhibitors have been reported as the main cause of life-threatening interactions with MDMA, citing three items from 1998, 1999 and 2012; by their titles two are about ritonavir and one is a letter on a fatal MDMA intoxication, and none names an MAO inhibitor.
key_findings.locator: MDMA drug-drug interactions, 3rd paragraph; reference list (Henry and Hill 1998; de la Torre et al. 1999; Papaseit et al. 2012)

key_findings.finding: Conclusion: the polymorphism and co-administered CYP2D6 inhibitors may have less impact on the risk of acute toxicity than previously thought, because other enzymes and renal excretion matter and because MDMA phenocopies everyone; clinical relevance of the polymorphism is called lower than predicted by in vitro studies. The Concluding remarks also say that carriers of reduced-function alleles are at higher risk of heightened effects, and that with environmental factors this may lead to acute toxicity including death.

In vitro background (Table 1 and the background section, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs): MDMA binds CYP2D6 with Km 2.2 (SD 1.6) and Ki 0.6 (SD 0.6) micromol/L, methamphetamine with Km 39.6 (SD 4.7) and Ki 25.0; the *1 enzyme variant clears MDMA 123 times faster than the *10 variant in vitro, and the review states without citation that *10 is carried by about 75% of Asian populations.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, MDMA and methamphetamine rows; CYP2D6, MDMA, and methamphetamine: background considerations, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Methamphetamine sections (summary only): CYP2D6 reduced-function genotypes were associated with lower odds of methamphetamine dependence in 202 Japanese patients against 337 controls (odds ratio 0.62 for intermediate metabolizers); extensive metabolizers did worse on cognitive tests in 52 people; bupropion, a CYP2D6 inhibitor, raised methamphetamine levels and lowered its effects in two trials.
key_findings.locator: Methamphetamine and CYP2D6 pharmacogenetics, 1st and 4th paragraphs; Methamphetamine drug-drug interaction, 1st paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: No methods are reported: the review does not say how studies were found or chosen. The Introduction promises to see how far three postulates (on abuse risk, neurotoxicity and toxicity in poor metabolizers) were confirmed, but the Concluding remarks do not give a verdict on each.
reporting_issues.consequence: Completeness cannot be judged and the conclusions cannot be traced to a stated body of evidence.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says everyone, irrespective of genotype or phenotype, is turned into a poor metabolizer by MDMA, and the Concluding remarks say all subjects are put at risk; the body reports phenocopying in 67% of men and 100% of women, with no denominators, from two studies by the authors' group. The 67% is 10 of 15 men in the 2008 study (read separately): after MDMA their urinary dextromethorphan to dextrorphan ratio was above the poor-metabolizer cut-off, and 5 men stayed below it.
reporting_issues.consequence: The headline fraction is stronger than the numbers given: in the one study that was read a third of the men did not reach poor-metabolizer values; the figures should be cited as the review's account of two small studies, not as a finding for everyone.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says the CYP2D6 share of clearance is substantially lower than expected from in vitro studies, but the in vitro expectation is never stated. The share itself is written three ways with different denominators: about 30% of metabolism, less than 30%, and lower than 50% of metabolic clearance (itself about 75% of plasma clearance).
reporting_issues.consequence: 'Lower than predicted' cannot be checked from the review; the share of MDMA clearance that depends on CYP2D6 is an approximate figure of the order of a quarter to a third, second-hand.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says MDMA is oxidized at almost 100 times the rate of methamphetamine and points to Table 1, but Table 1 gives affinity constants (Km 2.2 against 39.6 micromol/L, about 18-fold; Ki 0.6 against 25.0, about 42-fold), not rates. The 'almost 100-fold' difference between enzyme variants is a spread of 123 (MDMA) and 67 and 157 (two methamphetamine reactions). The figure of about 75% for the *10 variant in Asian populations has no citation.
reporting_issues.consequence: The in vitro comparisons are loosely summarized and should not be quoted as rates; they say nothing about the size of the effect in people.

reporting_issues.issue: A sentence says poor-metabolizer subjects show higher MDMA concentrations and a higher risk of hyperthermia after a single dose and has no citation; the next sentence cites a 2000 paper whose reference-list title is an in vitro study of the enzymes involved (Kreth et al.) for 'a similar observation' with MDE, another drug. The comparison of nine extensive metabolizers with poor metabolizers appears to rest on a 2005 paper whose title names one poor metabolizer.
reporting_issues.consequence: The claim of higher hyperthermia risk in poor metabolizers has no identifiable source in people; a single person is described in the plural.

reporting_issues.issue: The sentence on antidepressants that block CYP2D6 reads 'produce 15-30% of MDMA concentrations' with no verb, names no outcome (peak or exposure) and gives no per-medicine figures; the explanation of the lower effects ('probably' transporter competition) is a hypothesis.
reporting_issues.consequence: The range cannot be matched to a medicine or measure without the primary papers; the library reads the direction as an increase from the following sentence and from the review of trials.

reporting_issues.issue: MAO inhibitors are named, with ritonavir, as the main cause of life-threatening interactions with MDMA, but the three citations do not name an MAO inhibitor by title, no cases or denominators are given, and the paragraph does not say what the reactions were.
reporting_issues.consequence: The statement about MAO inhibitors is unsupported in this review; the ritonavir part rests on case reports.

reporting_issues.issue: The Concluding remarks state that carriers of reduced-function alleles are at higher risk of heightened effects and, with environmental factors, of acute toxicity including death, while the body reports no excess of poor-metabolizer genotypes in a series of poisonings and says the enzyme is blocked in everyone after a dose. The belief that poor metabolizers are under-represented among people who use MDMA is offered without data.
reporting_issues.consequence: The conclusions pull in opposite directions; neither is backed by genotype-specific data on toxicity or deaths.

reporting_issues.issue: For methamphetamine, an odds ratio of 0.62 with a 95% interval of 0.51 to 0.76 is printed beside p = 0.02. That interval implies p well below 0.001, and an interval this narrow is not possible from a simple two-group comparison of 202 patients with 337 controls (the narrowest possible at that odds ratio is about 0.44 to 0.88, editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: The interval or the sample sizes are misreported in the review; it concerns methamphetamine only and no MDMA claim uses it.

reporting_issues.issue: The review says MDMA inactivates most hepatic CYP2D6 'within 2 h' and that subjects show the poor-metabolizer phenotype within 2 hours, and gives the 2008 and 2011 studies as the source. In the 2008 study the first probe dose was given 4 hours after MDMA, so it cannot show the state of the enzyme at 2 hours; the review also writes that activity returned to a basal level 'after at least 10 days', whereas that study's own Discussion says the ratio had not fully recovered by 10 days although its abstract says it recovered.
reporting_issues.consequence: The timing of enzyme blockade (2 hours) and its end (10 days) are the review's wording, not the measured times of the cited men: the early rise in probe-drug exposure at 4 hours mixes competition for the enzyme with its inactivation, and the recovery half-life depends on the model (46.6 hours one-phase, 103 hours two-phase).

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC3495276 (abstract, all ten headed sections, Table 1 and the reference list read as text in the reader's own browser tab; Figures 1 and 2, the metabolic schemes, were not viewed as images; the page text had no affiliations or funding statement). The article number 235 is printed in the citation line (Front Genet. 2012 Nov 12;3:235); the reference record for de-la-torre_2012 holds the volume but not the number. The 2008 study cited for the phenocopying figures was read in full separately (see its own card) and is used above to check the review's account of it.
